pr_title: make sort by multiple columns parallel

issue_context.title: `.sort()` (on multiple columns with many duplicates) is ~3x slower than pandas
issue_context.body:
#### What language are you using?

Python

#### Have you tried latest version of polars?

Yes

#### What language version are you using
python 3.9.7

#### Describe your bug.

Polars is faster than pandas with pretty much every operation, but `.sort()` is much slower. Not sure if this is a bug or if this is expected.

```python
import polars as pl
from polars import col
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from timeit import timeit
import string

np.random.seed(123)

letters = np.asarray(list(string.ascii_lowercase))
random_strings = np.random.choice(letters, 200)
for i in range(3):
    random_strings = np.char.add(random_strings, np.random.choice(letters, 200))

data_size = 1000000

polars_df = pl.DataFrame(dict(
    a = np.random.choice(random_strings, data_size),
    b = np.random.choice(np.arange(20), data_size)
))
pandas_df = polars_df.to_pandas()

fns = dict(
    polars = lambda: polars_df.sort(['a', 'b']),
    pandas = lambda: pandas_df.sort_values(by=['a', 'b'])
)

time_df = pl.concat([
    pl.DataFrame({'package': [key], 'time': [timeit(fn, number = 30)]})
    for key, fn in fns.items()
])
    
time_df.with_columns(col('time').round(3))
```

```
┌─────────┬────────┐
│ package ┆ time   │
│ ---     ┆ ---    │
│ str     ┆ f64    │
╞═════════╪════════╡
│ polars  ┆ 13.924 │
├╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┤
│ pandas  ┆ 4.198  │
└─────────┴────────┘
```
comments:
Thanks for the report. It seems to be only the case on multiple columns when there are many duplicates.

If I sort only by a single column, polars is faster. 
If I increase the sample size of the intergers, polars is faster.

```python
polars_df = pl.DataFrame(dict(
    a = np.random.choice(random_strings, data_size),
    b = np.random.choice(np.arange(200000000), data_size)
))
```

I will look into it, maybe we have an accidental slow edge case.

review_comments: I suspect this means `IsFloat` should be an unsafe trait (unsafe to implement). Otherwise safe user code can implement it incorrectly on some local type (on which they also implement PartialOrd), leading to a soundness issue.
Good call. We should make that trait unsafe indeed.

Documentation could also help understand what `IsFloat` means.

For example, I could define a local type for 2D points on the integer grid (`struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }`). This struct could have a partial ordering implementation (`a > b` iff `a.x > b.x && a.y > b.y`), returning `None` in some cases.

Implementing `IsFloat` _sounds_ easy in that case (it's not a float), but even then we shouldn't be implementing this trait at all here, since there is no easy way to properly behave in this sort function.

It's not meant to be public. It's only for polars physical  types.

It is public because its in one of our subcrates, but any user implementation can never be used here. Because we only get here via polars physical types.


But for correctness I will make it an unsafe trait.

Is it actually impossible to call this method on user-defined types?

`PolarsNumericType` can be implemented on local types. I haven't tried yet, but is it really impossible to build a `ChunkedArray<LocalType>` (or a `ChunkedArray<Option<LocalType>>`)?
Or maybe you want to ["seal" these traits](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/future-proofing.html) to make sure they cannot be implemented for local types.
Ah, yes that would indeed be an elegant solution for this!

> PolarsNumericType can be implemented on local types. I haven't tried yet, but is it really impossible to build a ChunkedArray<LocalType> (or a ChunkedArray<Option<LocalType>>)?

Yes, that would blow up very quickly. You would not get your type into arrow arrays.

This implementation is dangerous, as users could implement `PartialOrd for Option<LocalType>` in ways that disagree with this.

For example, a user could have a float wrapper `struct LocalType(f32)`, have `impl PartialOrd for LocalType` by just forwarding the call to the wrapped float, and correctly implement `IsFloat for LocalType`. This code would look totally fine under review.

They could _also_ (arguably correctly) implement `PartialOrd for Option<LocalType>` by returning `None` if either of the two compared values is `None`. Here again, nothing looks unusual during an audit.

Still, this would lead to a possible soundness issue if attempting to sort values of type `Option<LocalType>`.
I will make it an unsafe trait. For all types this is intended to be used for this is correct.
